TB is found in the U.S., but it is more common in certain other countries. What causes tuberculosis (TB)? TB is caused by bacteria (germs) called Mycobacterium tuberculosis . The germs spread from person to person through the air. People who have TB disease in their throat or lungs spread the germs in the air when they cough, sneeze, talk, or sing. If you breathe in the air that has the germs, you can get TB. TB is not spread by touching, kissing, or sharing food or dishes. You're more likely to catch TB from people you live or work with than from people you see for shorter amounts of time. Who is more likely to get infected with tuberculosis (TB) germs? Anyone who is near a person with TB disease can get infected with the germs. You are more likely to be near someone with TB disease if you: Were born in or often travel to countries where TB disease is common Are a health care worker Work or live in a place where TB is more common, such as shelters for people without homes, jails, and nursing homes Who is more likely to develop TB disease? Certain people are more likely to get sick with TB disease after they get infected. They include people who: Have HIV Became infected with TB in the last 2 years Have other diseases, such as diabetes , that make it hard for your body to fight TB germs Have alcohol use disorder (AUD) or inject illegal drugs Were not treated correctly for TB in the past Are under age 5 Are an older adult Take medicines that weaken the immune system , such as medicines taken after an organ transplant , steroids , and specialized treatments for certain autoimmune diseases What are the symptoms of tuberculosis (TB)? Most people who have TB germs in their bodies don't get sick with TB disease. Instead, they have inactive TB infection. With an inactive TB infection, you: Don't have symptoms Can't spread TB to others Could get sick with active TB disease

b3_contexts: Arthritis On this page Basics Summary Start Here Diagnosis and Tests Treatments and Therapies Learn More Living With Related Issues Specifics Genetics See, Play and Learn Test Your Knowledge Research Statistics and Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Find an Expert For You Patient Handouts Summary What is arthritis? If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have arthritis. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called arthritis. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee. Most types of arthritis can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of arthritis can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of arthritis you have. What are the types of arthritis? Common types of arthritis include: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It's often related to aging or injury. Autoimmune arthritis happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake. Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of this type of arthritis. Juvenile arthritis is a type of arthritis that happens in children. Infectious arthritis is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive arthritis is one type. Psoriatic arthritis affects people with psoriasis (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches). Gout is a painful type of arthritis that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected. Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend. What are the symptoms of arthritis? Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common arthritis symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever , weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash. Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of arthritis may be signs of other illnesses. Who is more likely to get arthritis? A few things that might increase your chance of getting arthritis include: Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of arthritis if a member of your family has the disorder. Age. The risk of getting many types of arthritis increases with age. Sex. Certain types of arthritis are more common in women, while other types are more common in men. Other factors that might increase your risk of getting arthritis include having a previous joint injury, obesity , or lupus . How is arthritis diagnosed? To find out if you have arthritis, your health care provider may: Ask you about your medical history, including your symptoms. Do a physical exam. Order blood tests or take x-rays . Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in arthritis care) for tests, diagnosis, and

question: How many more Soil Health Cards were issued in Cycle-II compared to Cycle-I?
ground_truth: Cycle-II issued 12,424,624 more Soil Health Cards (119,773,040 in Cycle-II minus 107,348,416 in Cycle-I) than Cycle-I.
triseva_answer:
1. Direct answer
The provided context does not contain information on the number of Soil Health Cards issued in Cycle-I or Cycle-II.

2. Scheme/advisory pointers
The Soil Health Card scheme provides farmers with soil nutrient status and fertilizer recommendations. Key parameters include pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrients. Farmers should apply balanced fertilizers based on SHC advice rather than using only urea, to improve yield and soil health.

Keeping in view the high cost involved in provisioning and managing orphan diseases, the policy encourages active engagement with non-government sector for addressing the situation. In order to provide access and financial protection at secondary and tertiary care levels, the policy proposes free drugs, free diagnostics and free emergency care services in all public hospitals. To address the growing challenges of urban health, the policy advocates scaling up National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) to cover the entire urban population within the next five years with sustained financing. For effectively handling medical disasters and health security, the policy recommends that the public healthcare system retain a certain excess capacity in terms of health infrastructure, human resources, and technology which can be mobilized in times of crisis. In order to leverage the pluralistic health care legacy, the policy recommends mainstreaming the different health systems. This would involve increasing the validation, evidence and research of the different health care systems as a part of the common pool of knowledge. It would also involve providing access and informed choice to the patients, providing an enabling environment for practice of different systems of medicine, an enabling regulatory framework and encouraging cross referrals across these systems. 10 National Health Policy 2017 3.3.1 Primary Care Services and Continuity of Care This policy denotes important change from very selective to comprehensive primary health care package which includes geriatric health care, palliative care and rehabilitative care services. The facilities which start providing the larger package of comprehensive primary health care will be called ‘Health and Wellness Centers’. Primary care must be assured. To make this a reality, every family would have a health card that links them to primary care facility and be eligible for a defined package of services anywhere in the country. The policy recommends that health centres be established on geographical norms apart from population norms. To provide comprehensive care, the policy recommends a matching human resources development strategy, effective logistics support system and referral backup. This would also necessitate upgradation of the existing sub-centres and reorienting PHCs to provide comprehensive set of preventive, promotive, curative and rehabilitative services. It would entail providing access to assured AYUSH healthcare services, as well as support documentation and validation of local home and community based practices. The policy also advocates for research and validation of tribal medicines. Leveraging the potential of digital health for two way systemic linkages between the various levels of care viz., primary, secondary and tertiary,would ensure continuity of care. The policy advocates that the public health system would put in place a gatekeeping mechanism at primary level in a phased manner, accompanied by an effective feedback and follow-up mechanism. 3.3.2 Secondary Care Services The policy aspires to provide at the district level most of the secondary care which is currently provided at a medical college hospital. ground_truth: Transparency provisions ensure accountability and public oversight, while capacity building ensures that Panchayats and implementing bodies have the skills to execute the scheme effectively, creating a system with both oversight and competence.

Based on the provided context, the transparency provisions and capacity building components strengthen scheme implementation through the following mechanisms:

The State Council has the responsibility to promote widespread dissemination of information about the Act and its Schemes, while also monitoring implementation and coordinating with the Central Council.

Public authorities are required to publish comprehensive information including their organizational structure, functions, duties, rules, and budget allocations. This includes details about subsidy programs, beneficiaries, and electronic records. Information must be made accessible to citizens through various means, including electronic formats.

For implementation oversight, the District Programme Coordinator and implementing agencies bear responsibility for proper fund utilization. State Governments may establish requirements for maintaining proper records of employment and expenditures.

Payment procedures require that wages and unemployment allowances be made directly to recipients in the presence of independent community members on pre-announced dates. A complaint redressal system exists where disputes are referred to Programme Officers, who must record complaints and resolve them within seven days.

The scheme includes specific transparency measures requiring display of work estimates, job card lists, employment details, and expenditure information at worksites and Gram Panchayat offices. Websites must comply with RTI Act requirements, and social audits are mandated to verify implementation and expenditure.

*   **Monitoring and Redressal:** The first document (Doc 1) establishes a body responsible for monitoring the scheme's implementation, reviewing redressal mechanisms, and promoting the dissemination of information about the Act.

**Capacity Building Components:**

While not explicitly labeled as "capacity building," the documents contain provisions that build the administrative and operational capacity of the implementing bodies:

*   **Defined Roles and Procedures:** The MGNREGA Act (Doc 3) designates a "Programme Officer" who is responsible for entering complaints into a register and disposing of them within seven days. This creates a clear procedural framework and assigns responsibility.
*   **Prescribed Systems:** The RTI Act (Doc 2) requires public authorities to computerize records and maintain manuals and instructions. This builds the technical and procedural capacity to manage and share information effectively.
*   **Accountability Mechanisms:** The MGNREGA Act (Doc 3) states that implementing agencies are responsible for the proper utilization of funds and that the State Government can prescribe the manner of maintaining proper books of accounts. This builds financial management capacity.

Based on the provided context, the transparency provisions and capacity building components work together to create a system of accountability and informed participation, which strengthens the scheme's implementation.

Here is how they function together:

**1. Transparency Provisions Create the Framework for Accountability:**
The Act mandates several transparency measures to ensure the scheme's operations are open to public scrutiny. These include:
*   **Public Access to Records:** All accounts, records, and muster rolls must be made available for public scrutiny free of cost.
*   **Public Access to Reports:** Annual reports containing facts, figures, and achievements must be made available to the public on demand.
*   **Timely Information:** Copies of relevant extracts from these records must be provided within three working days of a request.

These provisions empower citizens and civil society to monitor the scheme's implementation directly.

**2. Capacity Building Components Enable Effective Participation and Implementation:**
The Act also mandates plans to build the capacity of both the implementing bodies and the beneficiaries. These include:
*   **Capacity Building Plan:** To enhance the skills of officials involved in the scheme.
*   **Information Education Communication (IEC) Plan:** To inform and educate people about the scheme.
*   **Plan for Strengthening Panchayats:** To empower local self-governance institutions.

**How They Work Together:**

The transparency provisions would be ineffective without the capacity building components. The **IEC plan** is the direct link, as it educates beneficiaries about their rights and how to access the information made transparent by the Act (e.g., how to request a copy of a muster roll or an annual report).

Similarly, the **Capacity Building Plan** ensures that officials like the Programme Officer and Gram Panchayat members have the skills to maintain accurate records and prepare the required reports. This makes the information provided to the public reliable and meaningful.

Finally, the **plan for strengthening Panchayats** empowers local bodies to act as effective intermediaries, helping citizens navigate the system and ensuring that the transparency and capacity building initiatives are implemented effectively at the grassroots level.

In essence, transparency provisions open the "books" of the scheme, while capacity building ensures that both the officials managing the books and the citizens reading them have the necessary knowledge and skills to make the process work, thereby strengthening the overall implementation of the scheme.

question: तपेदिक (टीबी) क्या है और यह शरीर के किस हिस्से पर आमतौर पर हमला करता है?
ground_truth: तपेदिक (टीबी) एक जीवाणु रोग है जो आमतौर पर फेफड़ों पर हमला करता है, लेकिन यह शरीर के अन्य हिस्सों पर भी हमला कर सकता है, जिनमें गुर्दे, रीढ़ की हड्डी और मस्तिष्क शामिल हैं।
triseva_answer:
प्रदान किए गए संदर्भ की समीक्षा करने के बाद, मुझे यह सूचित करना चाहिए कि संदर्भ में तपेदिक (टीबी) क्या है या यह शरीर के किस हिस्से पर हमला करता है, इसके बारे में कोई व्याख्यात्मक जानकारी नहीं है। संदर्भ में केवल तपेदिक से संबंधित विषयों, परीक्षणों और संसाधनों की एक सूची है, लेकिन इसमें वास्तविक चिकित्सा जानकारी या परिभाषाएँ शामिल नहीं हैं।

संदर्भ में निम्नलिखित सूचीबद्ध हैं:
- तपेदिक से संबंधित विषय (सक्रिय, औषधि-प्रतिरोधी, निष्क्रिय)
- तपेदिक से संबंधित परीक्षण (एसिड-फास्ट स्टेन, पीपीडी स्किन टेस्ट, थूक संवर्धन)
- विशिष्ट जनसंख्या (बच्चे, गर्भवती महिलाएं)
- संबंधित स्वास्थ्य विषय (माइकोबैक्टीरियल संक्रमण)

हालाँकि, संदर्भ में इस बारे में कोई विवरण नहीं है कि तपेदिक क्या है या यह शरीर के किस हिस्से को प्रभावित करता है।

कृपया व्यक्तिगत चिकित्सा सलाह के लिए एक योग्य डॉक्टर से परामर्श लें।

b3_contexts: Normal haemoglobin levels: Men 13.5-17.5 g/dL, Women 12.0-15.5 g/dL, Children 11.0-16.0 g/dL. Low haemoglobin is called anaemia. Common causes include iron deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, and chronic disease. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, and shortness of breath.

Metformin is a medication used to treat type 2 diabetes. It works by reducing glucose production in the liver and improving insulin sensitivity. Common side effects include nausea, diarrhoea, and stomach upset. It should be taken with meals. Normal fasting blood sugar: 70-100 mg/dL. Diabetic range: above 126 mg/dL fasting.

A fever is a body temperature above 38°C (100.4°F). Common causes include viral infections, bacterial infections, and inflammation. Treatment includes rest, hydration, and paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever above 38.5°C. Seek immediate medical care if fever exceeds 40°C, or is accompanied by severe headache, stiff neck, or difficulty breathing.

question: How long does treatment typically last for inactive TB infection?
ground_truth: Treatment for inactive TB infection usually lasts three, four, six, or nine months, depending on the treatment plan.

*   A 3-month course of isoniazid and rifapentine.
*   A 4-month course of rifampin.
*   A 9-month course of isoniazid.

The specific treatment plan depends on various factors, including the patient's age, risk of developing active TB, and potential drug interactions. A healthcare provider will determine the most appropriate course of treatment.

b3_contexts: Tuberculosis Also called: TB On this page Basics Summary Start Here Symptoms Diagnosis and Tests Prevention and Risk Factors Treatments and Therapies Learn More Related Issues Specifics See, Play and Learn No links available Research Statistics and Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Reference Desk Find an Expert For You Children Women Patient Handouts Summary What is tuberculosis (TB)? Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial disease that usually attacks the lungs. But it can also attack other parts of the body, including the kidneys, spine, and brain. Not everyone infected with TB bacteria (germs) becomes sick. So, there are two types of TB conditions: Inactive (latent) TB infection , where the TB germs live in your body but don't make you sick. TB disease (active TB) where you get sick from the TB germs. TB disease can almost always be cured with antibiotics . But if it's not treated properly, it can be fatal. TB is found in the U.S., but it is more common in certain other countries. What causes tuberculosis (TB)? TB is caused by bacteria (germs) called Mycobacterium tuberculosis . The germs spread from person to person through the air. People who have TB disease in their throat or lungs spread the germs in the air when they cough, sneeze, talk, or sing. If you breathe in the air that has the germs, you can get TB. TB is not spread by touching, kissing, or sharing food or dishes. You're more likely to catch TB from people you live or work with than from people you see for shorter amounts of time. Who is more likely to get infected with tuberculosis (TB) germs? Anyone who is near a person with TB disease can get infected with the germs. You are more likely to be near someone with TB disease if you: Were born in or often travel to countries where TB disease is common Are a health care worker Work or live in a place where TB is more common, such as shelters for people without homes, jails, and nursing homes Who is more likely to develop TB disease? Certain people are more likely to get sick with TB disease after they get infected. They include people who: Have HIV Became infected with TB in the last 2 years Have other diseases, such as diabetes , that make it hard for your body to fight TB germs Have alcohol use disorder (AUD) or inject illegal drugs Were not treated correctly for TB in the past Are under age 5 Are an older adult Take medicines that weaken the immune system , such as medicines taken after an organ transplant , steroids , and specialized treatments for certain autoimmune diseases What are the symptoms of tuberculosis (TB)? Most people who have TB germs in their bodies don't get sick with TB disease. Instead, they have inactive TB infection. With an inactive TB infection, you: Don't have symptoms Can't spread TB to others Could get sick with active TB disease

question: What is the significance of counting employment days provided during a calamity towards the 100-day guarantee?
ground_truth: It ensures that workers displaced by calamities are not disadvantaged and their employment during relocation counts toward their guaranteed 100 days of employment per household.
triseva_answer:
The number of days of employment provided during a national calamity is counted while computing the 100 days of guaranteed employment per household.

Source: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)

Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) guarantees 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households. Eligibility: adult members of rural households willing to do unskilled manual work. Wage rate varies by state. Work must be provided within 15 days of application, failing which unemployment allowance is paid. Apply at local Gram Panchayat.
b1_answer:
Based on the provided context, the significance of counting employment days provided during a calamity towards the 100-day guarantee is to ensure that the worker's entitlement is not disrupted.

The documents state that "The number of days of employment so provided shall be counted while computing 100 days of guaranteed employment per household." This means that if a rural household is displaced by a national calamity and its members find work in a temporary location, the days they work there are still counted towards their annual guarantee of 100 days of employment. This ensures they can continue to earn wages and fulfill their entitlement even during a crisis, without having to start over once normalcy is restored.

Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) guarantees 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households. Eligibility: adult members of rural households willing to do unskilled manual work. Wage rate varies by state. Work must be provided within 15 days of application, failing which unemployment allowance is paid. Apply at local Gram Panchayat.

Based on general knowledge of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), the significance of counting employment days provided during a calamity towards the 100-day guarantee is as follows:

The Act allows for the 100-day employment guarantee to be extended during periods of drought, flood, or other natural calamities. The significance of this provision is multi-fold:

1.  **Enhanced Social Security:** It provides a crucial safety net for rural households that have lost their primary sources of income or assets due to the disaster. It ensures they have a legal right to employment when they are most vulnerable.
2.  **Demand-Driven Employment:** It ensures that the demand for work is met even during a crisis, preventing distress migration from rural areas to cities in search of work.
3.  **Asset Creation and Resilience:** The work undertaken during such periods is often directly related to disaster mitigation and management, such as water conservation, drought-proofing, and flood control. This not only provides immediate employment but also helps build long-term community resilience against future calamities.
4.  **Legal Mandate for Action:** It provides a clear legal framework for the government to mobilize resources and provide employment beyond the standard 100-day limit, ensuring a more organized and effective response to the crisis.

question: What is a TIA and how does it relate to stroke risk?
ground_truth: A TIA (transient ischemic attack) or 'mini-stroke' occurs when blood supply to the brain is temporarily blocked. While brain damage isn't permanent, having a TIA significantly increases the risk of having a full stroke.
triseva_answer: A transient ischemic attack (TIA), sometimes called a "mini-stroke," is a condition similar to a stroke. It happens when the blood supply to the brain is blocked for a short time. While the damage to the brain cells isn't permanent, having a TIA puts you at a much higher risk of having a stroke.
triseva_contexts: Stroke Also called: Brain attack, CVA On this page Basics Summary Start Here Symptoms Diagnosis and Tests Prevention and Risk Factors Treatments and Therapies Learn More Living With Related Issues Specifics Genetics See, Play and Learn Images Videos and Tutorials Research Statistics and Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Reference Desk Find an Expert For You Children Women Older Adults Patient Handouts Summary What is a stroke? A stroke happens when there is a loss of blood flow to part of the brain. Your brain cells cannot get the oxygen and nutrients they need from blood, and they start to die within a few minutes. This can cause lasting brain damage, long-term disability, or even death. If you think that you or someone else is having a stroke, call 911 right away. Immediate treatment may save someone's life and increase the chances for successful rehabilitation and recovery. What are the types of stroke? There are two types of stroke: Ischemic stroke is caused by a blood clot that blocks or plugs a blood vessel in the brain. This is the most common type; about 80% of strokes are ischemic. Hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a blood vessel that breaks and bleeds into the brain. Another condition that's similar to a stroke is a transient ischemic attack (TIA). It's sometimes called a "mini-stroke." TIAs happen when the blood supply to the brain is blocked for a short time. The damage to the brain cells isn't permanent, but having a TIA puts you at much higher risk of having a stroke. Who is at risk for a stroke? Certain factors can raise your risk of a stroke. The major risk factors include: High blood pressure . This is the primary risk factor for a stroke. Diabetes . Heart diseases . Atrial fibrillation and other heart diseases can cause blood clots that lead to stroke. Smoking . When you smoke, you damage your blood vessels and raise your blood pressure. A personal or family history of stroke or TIA Age. Your risk of stroke increases as you get older. Race and ethnicity. People who are African Americans or Hispanic have a higher risk of stroke. There are also other factors that are linked to a higher risk of stroke, such as: Alcohol and illegal drug use Not getting enough physical activity High cholesterol Unhealthy diet Having obesity What are the symptoms of a stroke? The symptoms of a stroke often happen quickly. They include: Sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg (especially on one side of the body) Sudden confusion, trouble speaking, or understanding speech Sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes Sudden difficulty walking, dizziness, loss of balance or coordination Sudden severe headache with no known cause The F.A.S.T. test can help you remember what to look for if you think someone is having a stroke. Think "FAST" and look for: F ace drooping on one side when smiling. A rm weakness occurs when the arms are raised,

A stroke happens when there is a loss of blood flow to part of the brain. Your brain cells cannot get the oxygen and nutrients they need from blood, and they start to die within a few minutes. This can cause lasting brain damage, long-term disability, or even death. If you think that you or someone else is having a stroke, call 911 right away. Immediate treatment may save someone's life and increase the chances for successful rehabilitation and recovery. What are the types of stroke? There are two types of stroke: Ischemic stroke is caused by a blood clot that blocks or plugs a blood vessel in the brain. This is the most common type; about 80% of strokes are ischemic. Hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a blood vessel that breaks and bleeds into the brain. Another condition that's similar to a stroke is a transient ischemic attack (TIA). It's sometimes called a "mini-stroke." TIAs happen when the blood supply to the brain is blocked for a short time. A personal or family history of stroke or TIA Age. Your risk of stroke increases as you get older. Race and ethnicity. People who are African Americans or Hispanic have a higher risk of stroke. question: What role does the government play beyond providing soil health cards?
ground_truth: The government not only lists down measures to improve soil quality but also employs experts to help farmers implement these corrective measures.
triseva_answer:
1. Direct answer
Beyond providing soil health cards, the government offers crop insurance through the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana and agricultural extension services via Krishi Vigyan Kendras.
triseva_contexts: Soil Health Card scheme provides farmers with soil nutrient status and fertilizer recommendations. Key parameters include pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrients. Farmers should apply balanced fertilizers based on SHC advice rather than using only urea, to improve yield and soil health.

Krishi Vigyan Kendras provide district-level support including soil testing, crop advisories, demonstration trials, and farmer training. Farmers should use KVK and state agriculture university advisories for local weather-based recommendations on seed variety, nutrient management, and pest control.

Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana offers crop insurance against yield losses due to natural calamities, pests, and diseases. Farmer premium is typically 2 percent for Kharif crops, 1.5 percent for Rabi crops, and 5 percent for commercial or horticulture crops, with remaining premium subsidized by governments.
b1_answer:
Based on the provided documents, the government plays several other significant roles beyond providing soil health cards, particularly in the areas of healthcare, employment, and disaster management.

**In Healthcare:**
According to the National Health Policy 2017, the government's role includes:
*   **Providing free services:** Offering free drugs, free diagnostics, and free emergency care services in all public hospitals at secondary and tertiary care levels.
*   **Expanding healthcare access:** Scaling up the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) to cover the entire urban population.
*   **Establishing new facilities:** Creating 'Health and Wellness Centers' to provide a comprehensive package of primary health care, including geriatric, palliative, and rehabilitative services.
*   **Mainstreaming different health systems:** Increasing the validation and research of different systems of medicine (like AYUSH), providing access to them, and creating an enabling regulatory framework.
*   **Ensuring health security:** Recommending that the public healthcare system retain excess capacity in terms of infrastructure, human resources, and technology to handle medical disasters and crises.

**In Employment and Social Security:**
The legal document outlines a government role in providing employment guarantees:
*   **Guaranteeing employment:** Operating a scheme that provides a legal guarantee of 100 days of employment per rural household.
*   **Managing job cards:** Mandating Gram Panchayats to register households, issue job cards, and supply information to Programme Officers.

**In Disaster Management and Relief:**
The government has specific roles during national calamities:
*   **Providing relief to displaced populations:** Allowing adult members of rural households affected by disasters like floods or earthquakes to seek registration and get job cards in their area of temporary relocation.
*   **Ensuring continuity of benefits:** Counting the days of employment provided during displacement towards the 100-day guaranteed employment.
*   **Managing healthcare during crises:** Retaining excess capacity in the public healthcare system that can be mobilized during health emergencies.

The disease is mostly a problem in developing countries with warm climates. If you travel to these countries, you are at risk. question: What is the relationship between gestational diabetes and Type 2 diabetes risk?
ground_truth: Gestational diabetes usually goes away after pregnancy, but women who have had gestational diabetes have a higher risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later in life.
triseva_answer: Gestational diabetes usually goes away after you give birth. But you will have a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes later.

Ask your provider about the best way to check your blood glucose level and how often you should check it. Can diabetes be prevented? Type 1 diabetes can't be prevented. You may be able to delay or prevent type 2 diabetes through the same lifestyle changes that are used to manage diabetes (eating a healthy diet, staying at a healthy weight, and getting regular physical activity). प्रदत्त दस्तावेजों में मुझे इसका उत्तर नहीं मिल सका।

हालाँकि, सामान्य ज्ञान के आधार पर, तपेदिक (टीबी) का कारण बनने वाला जीवाणु *माइकोबैक्टीरियम ट्यूबरकुलोसिस* (*Mycobacterium tuberculosis*) है।
b3_contexts: Normal haemoglobin levels: Men 13.5-17.5 g/dL, Women 12.0-15.5 g/dL, Children 11.0-16.0 g/dL. Low haemoglobin is called anaemia. Common causes include iron deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, and chronic disease. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, and shortness of breath.

Metformin is a medication used to treat type 2 diabetes. It works by reducing glucose production in the liver and improving insulin sensitivity. Common side effects include nausea, diarrhoea, and stomach upset. It should be taken with meals. Normal fasting blood sugar: 70-100 mg/dL. Diabetic range: above 126 mg/dL fasting.

A fever is a body temperature above 38°C (100.4°F). Common causes include viral infections, bacterial infections, and inflammation. Treatment includes rest, hydration, and paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever above 38.5°C. Seek immediate medical care if fever exceeds 40°C, or is accompanied by severe headache, stiff neck, or difficulty breathing.

However, based on general medical knowledge, here are some diagnostic tests a healthcare provider might use to diagnose a stroke:

*   **Neurological Exam:** A physical exam to check vision, coordination, balance, reflexes, and mental status.
*   **CT Scan (Computed Tomography):** A fast and common imaging test to create detailed pictures of the brain and determine if the stroke is caused by bleeding (hemorrhagic) or a clot (ischemic).
*   **MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging):** Provides a more detailed image of the brain and can help identify the exact location and extent of brain damage.
*   **Blood Tests:** To check for clotting disorders, blood sugar levels, and other factors that could contribute to a stroke.
*   **Carotid Ultrasound:** Uses sound waves to create images of the carotid arteries in the neck to check for narrowing or blockages.

When you are having an asthma attack, your symptoms get much worse. The attacks may come on gradually or suddenly. Sometimes they can be life-threatening. They are more common in people who have severe asthma. If you are having asthma attacks, you may need a change in your treatment. How is asthma diagnosed? Your health care provider may use many tools to diagnose asthma: Physical exam Medical history Lung function tests , including spirometry, to test how well your lungs work Tests to measure how your airways react to specific exposures. During this test, you inhale different concentrations of allergens or medicines that may tighten the muscles in your airways. Spirometry is done before and after the test. Peak expiratory flow (PEF) tests to measure how fast you can blow air out using maximum effort Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) tests to measure levels of nitric oxide in your breath when you breathe out. High levels of nitric oxide may mean that your lungs are inflamed. Allergy skin or blood tests, if you have a history of allergies. These tests check which allergens cause a reaction from your immune system. What are the treatments for asthma? If you have asthma, you will work with your health care provider to create a treatment plan. The plan will include ways to manage your asthma symptoms and prevent asthma attacks. It will include: Strategies to avoid triggers. For example, if tobacco smoke is a trigger for you, you should not smoke or allow other people to smoke in your home or car. Short-term relief medicines, also called quick-relief medicines. They help prevent symptoms or relieve symptoms during an asthma attack. They include an inhaler to carry with you all the time. It may also include other types of medicines which work quickly to help open your airways. Control medicines. You take them every day to help prevent symptoms. They work by reducing airway inflammation and preventing narrowing of the airways. If you have a severe attack and the short-term relief medicines do not work, you will need emergency care. Your provider may adjust your treatment until asthma symptoms are controlled. Sometimes asthma is severe and cannot be controlled with other treatments. If you are an adult with uncontrolled asthma, in some cases your provider might suggest bronchial thermoplasty. This is a procedure that uses heat to shrink the smooth muscle in the lungs. Shrinking the muscle reduces your airway's ability to tighten and allows you to breathe more easily. The procedure has some risks, so it's important to discuss them with your provider. question: Arthritis ke teen common types batao.
ground_truth: Arthritis ke teen common types hain osteoarthritis (sabse common type), rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune arthritis ka sabse common form), aur gout (excess uric acid buildup se hota hai).
triseva_answer:
Arthritis ke teen common types hain:

1.  **Osteoarthritis:** Yeh arthritis ka sabse common type hai. Yeh aksar aging ya injury se related hota hai.
2.  **Autoimmune arthritis:** Yeh tab hota hai jab body ka immune system galti se healthy cells par attack karta hai. Rheumatoid arthritis iska sabse common form hai.
3.  **Juvenile arthritis:** Yeh ek type ka arthritis hai jo bachon mein hota hai.

If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have arthritis. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called arthritis. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee. Most types of arthritis can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of arthritis can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of arthritis you have. What are the types of arthritis? Common types of arthritis include: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It's often related to aging or injury. Autoimmune arthritis happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake. Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of this type of arthritis. Juvenile arthritis is a type of arthritis that happens in children. Infectious arthritis is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive arthritis is one type. Psoriatic arthritis affects people with psoriasis (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches). Gout is a painful type of arthritis that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected. Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend. Other symptoms could include fever , weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash. Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of arthritis may be signs of other illnesses. b2_answer:
1. Direct answer — In the Jharkhand identification process, village and circle level revenue officials verify and authenticate the 'Vanshavali' (lineage chart) and the possession of the land holding.
2. Key eligibility criteria — For identification in Jharkhand, a farmer must submit a 'Vanshavali' (lineage chart) linked to land records. This chart is first submitted to the Gram Sabha for approval. After Gram Sabha approval, the village and circle level revenue officials verify and authenticate the Vanshavali and the farmer's possession of the land holding.
3. Required documents — The 'Vanshavali' (lineage chart) linked to the land record is the required document for this specific identification process in Jharkhand.
4. How to apply — The process involves submitting the lineage chart to the Gram Sabha for approval. Following this, the village and circle level revenue officials verify and authenticate the document and land possession.
5. Source: PM-Kisan Operational Guidelines

question: Why are people who travel frequently to certain countries at higher risk of TB infection?
ground_truth: People who travel to countries where TB disease is common are more likely to be near someone with active TB disease and therefore have a higher chance of breathing in TB germs and becoming infected.
triseva_answer:
According to the provided information, people who often travel to countries where TB disease is common are at a higher risk of infection because they are more likely to be near someone with active TB disease.

Relevant medical context:
The context states that you are more likely to be near someone with TB disease if you "were born in or often travel to countries where TB disease is common." The germs that cause TB spread through the air when a person with active TB disease in their lungs coughs, sneezes, talks, or sings.

Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial disease that usually attacks the lungs. But it can also attack other parts of the body, including the kidneys, spine, and brain. Not everyone infected with TB bacteria (germs) becomes sick. So, there are two types of TB conditions: Inactive (latent) TB infection , where the TB germs live in your body but don't make you sick. TB disease (active TB) where you get sick from the TB germs. TB disease can almost always be cured with antibiotics . But if it's not treated properly, it can be fatal. TB is found in the U.S., but it is more common in certain other countries. What causes tuberculosis (TB)? TB is caused by bacteria (germs) called Mycobacterium tuberculosis . Diabetes, also known as diabetes mellitus, is a disease in which your blood glucose , or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose is your body's main source of energy. Your body can make glucose, but it also comes from the food you eat. Insulin is a hormone made by your pancreas. Insulin helps move glucose from your bloodstream into your cells, where it can be used for energy. If you have diabetes, your body can't make insulin, can't use insulin as well as it should, or both. Too much glucose stays in your blood and doesn't reach your cells. This can cause glucose levels to get too high. Over time, high blood glucose levels can lead to serious health conditions . But you can take steps to manage your diabetes and try to prevent these health problems. What are the types of diabetes? There are different types of diabetes: Type 1 diabetes . If you have type 1 diabetes, your body makes little or no insulin. It happens when your immune system attacks and destroys the cells that produce insulin. Type 2 diabetes . This is the most common form of diabetes. If you have type 2 diabetes, your body may still be able to make insulin, but your cells don't respond well to insulin. They can't easily take up enough glucose from your blood. Gestational diabetes . This is a form of diabetes that develops during pregnancy. It happens when your body can't make the extra insulin it needs during pregnancy. What causes diabetes? The different types of diabetes have different causes: Researchers think type 1 diabetes is caused by genes and factors in the environment that might trigger the disease. Type 2 diabetes is caused by several factors, including lifestyle factors and genes . The lifestyle factors include not being physically active and being overweight or having obesity . Researchers think gestational diabetes is caused by the hormonal changes of pregnancy along with genetic and lifestyle factors. Who is more likely to develop diabetes? The different types of diabetes have different risk factors: You can develop type 1 diabetes at any age, but it most often starts in childhood. Having a parent or sibling with type 1 diabetes may increase your chance of developing it. You are at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes if you: Are overweight or have obesity. Are over age 35. Children, teenagers, and younger adults can get diabetes, but it is more common in middle-aged and older adults. Have a family history of diabetes. Have prediabetes . question: What does the passage say about representing second-hand goods as new?
ground_truth: According to the passage, falsely representing rebuilt, second-hand, renovated, reconditioned, or old goods as new goods is an unfair trade practice.
triseva_answer:
The passage states that falsely representing second-hand goods as new goods is an unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice.

Source: Consumer Protection
triseva_contexts: for the purpose of promoting the sale, use or supply of any goods or for the provision of any service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice including any of the following practices, namely:— (i) making any statement, whether orally or in writing or by visible representation including by means of electronic record, which— (a) falsely represents that the goods are of a particular standard, quality, quantity, grade, composition, style or model; (b) falsely represents that the services are of a particular standard, quality or grade; (c) falsely represents any re-built, second-hand, renovated, reconditioned or old goods as new goods; (d) represents that the goods or services have sponsorship, approval, performance, characteristics, accessories, uses or benefits which such goods or services do not have; (e) represents that the seller or the supplier has a sponsorship or approval or affiliation which such seller or supplier does not have; (f) makes a false or misleading representation concerning the need for, or the usefulness of, any goods or services; (g) gives to the public any warranty or guarantee of the performance, efficacy or length of life of a product or of any goods that is not based on an adequate or proper test thereof: Provided that where a defence is raised to the effect that such warranty or guarantee is based on adequate or proper test, the burden of proof of such defence shall lie on the person raising such defence; (h) makes to the public a representation in a form that purports to be— (A) a warranty or guarantee of a product or of any goods or services; or (B) a promise to replace, maintain or repair an article or any part thereof or to repeat or continue a service until it has achieved a specified result, if such purported warranty or guarantee or promise is materially misleading or if there is no reasonable prospect that such warranty, guarantee or promise will be carried out; Central Consumer Protection Council.—(1) The Central Government shall, by notification, establish with effect from such date as it may specify in that notification, the Central Consumer Protection Council to be known as the Central Council. If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have arthritis. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called arthritis. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee. Most types of arthritis can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of arthritis can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of arthritis you have. What are the types of arthritis? Common types of arthritis include: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It's often related to aging or injury. Autoimmune arthritis happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake. Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of this type of arthritis. Juvenile arthritis is a type of arthritis that happens in children. Infectious arthritis is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive arthritis is one type. Psoriatic arthritis affects people with psoriasis (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches). Gout is a painful type of arthritis that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected. Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend. What are the symptoms of arthritis? Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common arthritis symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever , weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash. Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of arthritis may be signs of other illnesses. Who is more likely to get arthritis? A few things that might increase your chance of getting arthritis include: Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of arthritis if a member of your family has the disorder. Age. The risk of getting many types of arthritis increases with age. Sex. Certain types of arthritis are more common in women, while other types are more common in men. Other factors that might increase your risk of getting arthritis include having a previous joint injury, obesity , or lupus . How is arthritis diagnosed? To find out if you have arthritis, your health care provider may: Ask you about your medical history, including your symptoms. Do a physical exam. Order blood tests or take x-rays . Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in arthritis care) for tests, diagnosis, and

b1_answer:
Based on the provided documents, the following types of false statements about goods are considered unfair trade practices:

*   Falsely representing that the goods are of a particular standard, quality, quantity, grade, composition, style, or model.
*   Falsely representing any rebuilt, second-hand, renovated, reconditioned, or old goods as new goods.
*   Representing that the goods have sponsorship, approval, performance, characteristics, accessories, uses, or benefits which they do not have.
*   Making a false or misleading representation concerning the need for, or the usefulness of, the goods.
*   Giving a warranty or guarantee of the performance, efficacy, or length of life of a product that is not based on an adequate or proper test.
*   Making a representation that purports to be a warranty or guarantee, if it is materially misleading or there is no reasonable prospect it will be carried out.
*   Giving false or misleading facts that disparage the goods of another person.

ground_truth: The programme involves state/district agriculture departments, panchayats, village-level workers (Krishi Sakhis, Pasu Sakhis), and rural development workers to create a comprehensive network for farmer education and soil health management.

1. Direct answer
The implementation of the soil health programme involves multiple stakeholders. The Soil Health Card scheme provides farmers with soil nutrient status and fertilizer recommendations. Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) provide district-level support, including soil testing and crop advisories. State agriculture universities also contribute by offering local advisories.

2. Scheme/advisory pointers
- Soil Health Card scheme: Provides soil nutrient status and fertilizer recommendations.
- Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs): Offer soil testing, crop advisories, and farmer training.
- State agriculture university advisories: Provide local weather-based recommendations on seed variety, nutrient management, and pest control.

Integrated Pest Management promotes preventive and need-based control methods. Farmers should monitor fields regularly, use pest thresholds, prefer biological and mechanical controls first, and use chemical pesticides only when needed. b3_contexts: Arthritis On this page Basics Summary Start Here Diagnosis and Tests Treatments and Therapies Learn More Living With Related Issues Specifics Genetics See, Play and Learn Test Your Knowledge Research Statistics and Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Find an Expert For You Patient Handouts Summary What is arthritis? If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have arthritis. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called arthritis. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee. Most types of arthritis can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of arthritis can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of arthritis you have. What are the types of arthritis? Common types of arthritis include: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It's often related to aging or injury. Autoimmune arthritis happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake. Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of this type of arthritis. Juvenile arthritis is a type of arthritis that happens in children. Infectious arthritis is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive arthritis is one type. Psoriatic arthritis affects people with psoriasis (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches). Gout is a painful type of arthritis that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected. Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend. What are the symptoms of arthritis? Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common arthritis symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever , weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash. Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of arthritis may be signs of other illnesses. Who is more likely to get arthritis? A few things that might increase your chance of getting arthritis include: Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of arthritis if a member of your family has the disorder. Age. The risk of getting many types of arthritis increases with age. Sex. Certain types of arthritis are more common in women, while other types are more common in men. Other factors that might increase your risk of getting arthritis include having a previous joint injury, obesity , or lupus . How is arthritis diagnosed? If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have arthritis. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called arthritis. Common types of arthritis include: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It's often related to aging or injury. Autoimmune arthritis happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake. Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of this type of arthritis. Juvenile arthritis is a type of arthritis that happens in children. Infectious arthritis is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive arthritis is one type. However, based on general medical knowledge, here is an explanation of why an Indian woman of Hispanic/Latino ethnicity and age 36 who is overweight should be concerned about developing Type 2 diabetes:

Several key risk factors are present in this individual's profile, and their combination significantly increases the risk:

1.  **Overweight/Obesity:** This is one of the most significant risk factors for Type 2 diabetes. Excess body fat, particularly around the abdomen, contributes to insulin resistance, a condition where the body's cells don't respond effectively to the hormone insulin. This forces the pancreas to work harder to produce more insulin, and over time, it may not be able to keep up, leading to high blood sugar levels.

2.  **Ethnicity (Hispanic/Latino and Indian/South Asian):** Certain ethnic groups have a genetically higher predisposition to developing Type 2 diabetes.
    *   **Hispanic/Latino individuals** have a notably higher risk of developing Type 2 diabetes compared to non-Hispanic white individuals.
    *   **People of South Asian descent (including Indian)** also have a very high genetic risk. They often develop Type 2 diabetes at a younger age and at a lower body mass index (BMI) than other ethnic groups.

3.  **Age (36):** While the risk of Type 2 diabetes increases with age (typically after 45), it is increasingly being diagnosed in younger adults, especially those with other risk factors like being overweight and belonging to a high-risk ethnic group.

In summary, this individual has multiple, powerful risk factors. Being overweight significantly increases the risk, and this risk is amplified by her ethnicity, which carries a strong genetic predisposition. The combination of these factors at a relatively young age makes her a high-risk candidate for developing Type 2 diabetes. question: What is the difference between a 'rural area' and an urban area as defined in this Act?
ground_truth: A rural area means any area in a State except those areas covered by any urban local body or a Cantonment Board established under any law for the time being in force.
triseva_answer:
According to the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, a 'rural area' is defined as any area in a State except those areas covered by any urban local body or a Cantonment Board established or constituted under any law for the time being in force.

The Act does not provide a separate, explicit definition for 'urban area'. However, based on the definition of 'rural area', an 'urban area' is implicitly defined as an area that is covered by an 'urban local body' or a 'Cantonment Board'.

Source: MGNREGA

question: Why might the government be promoting customized and fortified fertilizers alongside the Soil Health Card scheme?
ground_truth: The government is promoting customized and fortified fertilizers to ensure balanced use of fertilizers based on soil health information, improving nutrient management and crop productivity.
triseva_answer:
The government promotes customized and fortified fertilizers alongside the Soil Health Card scheme to ensure farmers apply nutrients that are specifically required by their soil. The Soil Health Card provides a detailed analysis of soil parameters, including micronutrients, which standard fertilizers like urea may not address. This approach aims to replace the common practice of using only urea with a balanced application of nutrients to improve both crop yield and long-term soil health.

**Scheme/advisory pointers:**
The Soil Health Card scheme is the primary advisory tool. Farmers should use the fertilizer recommendations provided on their card to select the appropriate customized or fortified fertilizers for their specific field.
triseva_contexts: Soil Health Card scheme provides farmers with soil nutrient status and fertilizer recommendations. Key parameters include pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrients. Farmers should apply balanced fertilizers based on SHC advice rather than using only urea, to improve yield and soil health.

Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana offers crop insurance against yield losses due to natural calamities, pests, and diseases. Farmer premium is typically 2 percent for Kharif crops, 1.5 percent for Rabi crops, and 5 percent for commercial or horticulture crops, with remaining premium subsidized by governments.

Micro-irrigation systems such as drip and sprinkler can improve water-use efficiency and reduce input cost. Drip is suitable for row crops and horticulture, while sprinkler can support wider field coverage. States often provide subsidies under PMKSY components; farmers can apply through agriculture department portals.

Based on the provided documents, the government is promoting customized and fortified fertilizers alongside the Soil Health Card (SHC) scheme to address micronutrient deficiencies in both the soil and the population.

Here's the reasoning:

1.  **The Soil Health Card scheme identifies specific deficiencies:** As stated in Doc 1, the SHC scheme provides farmers with the soil's nutrient status, including key parameters like pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and **micronutrients**. The scheme advises farmers to apply "balanced fertilizers" based on this specific advice rather than using only urea.

2.  **The National Health Policy identifies micronutrient deficiencies as a public health crisis:** Doc 2 highlights that "micronutrient deficiencies" are a major problem that restricts the growth and development of children and contributes to morbidity and mortality. The policy calls for a "well-planned strategy on micronutrient interventions," including food fortification and supplementation.

3.  **The policies call for synergy between departments:** The National Health Policy (Doc 2) explicitly calls for "synergy of inputs from departments like Women and Child Development, Education, WASH, **Agriculture** and Food and Civil Supplies" to address nutrition.

Therefore, the promotion of customized fertilizers is a direct application of the SHC scheme's findings, allowing farmers to apply the precise nutrients their soil lacks. The promotion of fortified fertilizers is a broader strategy to ensure that essential micronutrients are added to the food supply, directly addressing the public health goals outlined in the National Health Policy. This integrated approach aims to improve soil health, crop yield, and ultimately, the nutritional status of the population.

Recognising this, the policy declares that micronutrient deficiencies would be addressed through a well-planned strategy on micronutrient interventions. Focus would be on reducing micronutrient malnourishment and augmenting initiatives like micro nutrient supplementation, food fortification, screening for anemia and public awareness. A systematic approach to address heterogeneity in micronutrient adequacy across regions in the country with focus on the more vulnerable sections of the population, is needed. Hence, screening for multiple micronutrient deficiencies is advocated. This includes not just nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, but also micronutrients. Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana offers crop insurance against yield losses due to natural calamities, pests, and diseases. Farmer premium is typically 2 percent for Kharif crops, 1.5 percent for Rabi crops, and 5 percent for commercial or horticulture crops, with remaining premium subsidized by governments.

Micro-irrigation systems such as drip and sprinkler can improve water-use efficiency and reduce input cost. Diabetes, also known as diabetes mellitus, is a disease in which your blood glucose , or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose is your body's main source of energy. Your body can make glucose, but it also comes from the food you eat. Insulin is a hormone made by your pancreas. Insulin helps move glucose from your bloodstream into your cells, where it can be used for energy. If you have diabetes, your body can't make insulin, can't use insulin as well as it should, or both. Too much glucose stays in your blood and doesn't reach your cells. This can cause glucose levels to get too high. Over time, high blood glucose levels can lead to serious health conditions . But you can take steps to manage your diabetes and try to prevent these health problems. What are the types of diabetes? There are different types of diabetes: Type 1 diabetes . If you have type 1 diabetes, your body makes little or no insulin. It happens when your immune system attacks and destroys the cells that produce insulin. Type 2 diabetes . This is the most common form of diabetes. If you have type 2 diabetes, your body may still be able to make insulin, but your cells don't respond well to insulin. They can't easily take up enough glucose from your blood. Gestational diabetes . This is a form of diabetes that develops during pregnancy. It happens when your body can't make the extra insulin it needs during pregnancy. What causes diabetes? The different types of diabetes have different causes: Researchers think type 1 diabetes is caused by genes and factors in the environment that might trigger the disease. Type 2 diabetes is caused by several factors, including lifestyle factors and genes . The lifestyle factors include not being physically active and being overweight or having obesity . Researchers think gestational diabetes is caused by the hormonal changes of pregnancy along with genetic and lifestyle factors. Who is more likely to develop diabetes? The different types of diabetes have different risk factors: You can develop type 1 diabetes at any age, but it most often starts in childhood. Having a parent or sibling with type 1 diabetes may increase your chance of developing it. You are at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes if you: Are overweight or have obesity. Are over age 35. Children, teenagers, and younger adults can get diabetes, but it is more common in middle-aged and older adults. Have a family history of diabetes. Have prediabetes . Thyroid Diseases On this page Basics Summary Start Here Diagnosis and Tests Treatments and Therapies Learn More Related Issues Specifics Genetics See, Play and Learn Images Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Find an Expert For You Children Women Older Adults Patient Handouts Summary Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck. It makes hormones that control the way the body uses energy. These hormones affect nearly every organ in your body and control many of your body's most important functions. For example, they affect your breathing, heart rate, weight, digestion, and moods. Thyroid diseases cause your thyroid to make either too much or too little of the hormones. Some of the different thyroid diseases include: Goiter, an enlargement of the thyroid gland Hyperthyroidism , which happens when your thyroid gland makes more thyroid hormones than your body needs Hypothyroidism , which happens when your thyroid gland does not make enough thyroid hormones Thyroid cancer Thyroid nodules, lumps in the thyroid gland Thyroiditis, swelling of the thyroid To diagnose thyroid diseases, your health care provider may use a medical history, physical exam, and thyroid tests . In some cases, your provider may also do a biopsy . Treatment depends on the problem, how severe it is, and what your symptoms are. Possible treatments may include medicines, radioiodine therapy, or thyroid surgery. Thyroid Diseases On this page Basics Summary Start Here Diagnosis and Tests Treatments and Therapies Learn More Related Issues Specifics Genetics See, Play and Learn Images Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Find an Expert For You Children Women Older Adults Patient Handouts Summary Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck. It makes hormones that control the way the body uses energy. These hormones affect nearly every organ in your body and control many of your body's most important functions. For example, they affect your breathing, heart rate, weight, digestion, and moods. Thyroid diseases cause your thyroid to make either too much or too little of the hormones. Some of the different thyroid diseases include: Goiter, an enlargement of the thyroid gland Hyperthyroidism , which happens when your thyroid gland makes more thyroid hormones than your body needs Hypothyroidism , which happens when your thyroid gland does not make enough thyroid hormones Thyroid cancer Thyroid nodules, lumps in the thyroid gland Thyroiditis, swelling of the thyroid To diagnose thyroid diseases, your health care provider may use a medical history, physical exam, and thyroid tests . In some cases, your provider may also do a biopsy . Treatment depends on the problem, how severe it is, and what your symptoms are. Possible treatments may include medicines, radioiodine therapy, or thyroid surgery. b3_contexts: Heart Diseases Also called: Cardiac diseases On this page Basics Summary Start Here Diagnosis and Tests Prevention and Risk Factors Treatments and Therapies Learn More Living With Related Issues Specifics Genetics See, Play and Learn Videos and Tutorials Test Your Knowledge Research Statistics and Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Reference Desk Find an Expert For You Children Men Women Older Adults Patient Handouts Summary What is heart disease? Heart disease is a general term that includes many types of heart problems. It's a type of cardiovascular disease, which means heart and blood vessel disease. Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the United States, but there are ways to prevent and manage many types of heart disease. What are the types of heart disease? There are many different types of heart disease. Some you may be born with, called congenital heart disease . Other types develop during your lifetime. Coronary artery disease (also called coronary heart disease) is the most common type of heart disease. It happens slowly over time when a sticky substance called plaque builds up in the arteries that supply your heart muscle with blood. The plaque narrows or blocks blood flow to the heart muscle and can lead to other heart problems: Angina - chest pain from lack of blood flow Heart attacks - when part of the heart muscle dies from loss of blood flow Heart failure - when your heart can't pump enough blood to meet your body's needs Arrhythmia - a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat Other types of heart diseases may affect your heart valves or heart muscle ( cardiomyopathy ). What causes heart diseases? The causes of heart disease depend on the type of disease. Some possible causes include lifestyle, genetics, infections, medicines, and other diseases. Who is more likely to develop heart diseases? There are many different factors that can make you more likely to develop heart disease. Some of these factors you can change, but others you cannot. Age. Your risk of heart disease goes up as you get older. Sex. Some factors may affect heart disease risk differently in women than in men. Family history and genetics. A family history of early heart disease raises your risk. And research has shown that some genes are linked to a higher risk of certain heart diseases. Race/ethnicity. Heart disease is the leading cause of death in most racial and ethnic groups in the United States. However, certain groups have higher risks than others. This includes Black people, White people, and American Indian/Alaska Native people. Lifestyle habits. Over time, unhealthy lifestyle habits can raise your risk of heart disease. These can include: Eating a diet high in saturated fats , refined carbohydrates, and salt . Not getting enough physical activity . Drinking too much alcohol . Smoking and exposure to secondhand smoke . Too much stress . Having other medical conditions can raise your risk of heart diseases. These conditions include: High blood pressure

However, based on general medical knowledge, patients with dengue fever are advised to avoid aspirin and ibuprofen because these medications can increase the risk of bleeding. Dengue can already cause a low platelet count and make blood vessels more fragile. Aspirin and ibuprofen are blood thinners, and taking them can worsen this bleeding risk, potentially leading to severe complications. Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is typically recommended as a safer alternative for managing fever and pain.

However, based on general medical knowledge, patients with dengue are advised to avoid aspirin and ibuprofen because these medications are nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) that can increase the risk of bleeding. Dengue infection can lead to a drop in platelet count and, in severe cases, cause internal bleeding. Taking aspirin or ibuprofen could worsen this bleeding risk. b3_contexts: Dengue Also called: Break-bone fever, Dengue fever On this page Basics Summary Start Here Symptoms Diagnosis and Tests Prevention and Risk Factors Learn More Related Issues See, Play and Learn No links available Research Statistics and Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Find an Expert For You Children Patient Handouts Summary What is dengue? Dengue is a viral infection . It can be caused by four related viruses. You can get it if an infected mosquito bites you. It is common in warm, wet areas of the world. Although rare, it can be found in some parts of the United States. Outbreaks are more common during rainy seasons. How does dengue spread? Dengue spreads to people through the bite of an infected mosquito. It does not spread directly from person to person. However, the infection can be passed to the baby during pregnancy. In rare cases, it can spread through a blood transfusion , organ transplant , or needle stick injury (an accidental injury from a used needle).. What are the symptoms of dengue and severe dengue? About one in four people infected with dengue will get sick. For those who do get sick, the infection can be mild or severe. The symptoms of dengue include: A high fever Nausea and vomiting Rash Aches and pains (eye pain, usually behind the eyes, and pain in the muscles, joints, or bones) The symptoms usually last two to seven days. Severe dengue is a serious form of the illness. About 1 in 20 people who get sick with dengue will develop severe dengue. It can cause shock , internal bleeding, and even death. People are more likely to develop severe dengue if they have had dengue before, are pregnant, or are infants. Watch for signs and symptoms of severe dengue. Warning signs usually begin about 24 - 48 hours after your fever has gone away. If you or your family member have these signs, get immediate medical care: Severe abdominal (belly) pain and tenderness Vomiting at least 3 times in 24 hours Bleeding from the nose or gums Vomiting blood, or blood in the stool (poop) Feeling tired, restless, or irritable How is dengue diagnosed? There is a blood test which can show if you have been infected with dengue. What are the treatments for dengue? There is no specific medicine to treat dengue. Most people will get better after about a week. But if you think you might have dengue: See a health care provider and mention any recent travel. Rest as much as possible. Take acetaminophen to control fever and relieve pain. But do not take aspirin or ibuprofen. Drink plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration . Severe dengue often requires care at a hospital. Can dengue be prevented? In the United States, a dengue vaccine is approved for children who are ages 9 - 16. They must also have previously had dengue and live in areas where dengue is common. You can also help prevent dengue by avoiding mosquito

गठिया (अर्थराइटिस) उन स्थितियों के लिए एक सामान्य शब्द है जिनमें जोड़ों में सूजन शामिल होती है। जोड़ों में दर्द, जकड़न और सूजन इसके सामान्य लक्षण हैं। गठिया के कई प्रकार हैं, जिनमें ऑस्टियोआर्थराइटिस (घिसावट के कारण होने वाला) और रूमेटाइड अर्थराइटिस (एक ऑटोइम्यून बीमारी) सबसे सामान्य हैं।

यह जानकारी सामान्य ज्ञान पर आधारित है और दिए गए दस्तावेजों से नहीं ली गई है।

Metformin is a medication used to treat type 2 diabetes. It works by reducing glucose production in the liver and improving insulin sensitivity. A fever is a body temperature above 38°C (100.4°F). Common causes include viral infections, bacterial infections, and inflammation. Treatment includes rest, hydration, and paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever above 38.5°C. Seek immediate medical care if fever exceeds 40°C, or is accompanied by severe headache, stiff neck, or difficulty breathing.

question: Why was 2015 significant for soil-related initiatives in India?
ground_truth: 2015 was significant because it was the International Year of Soils, and India launched the unique Soil Health Card Scheme in the same year to assess nutrient status across farm holdings.

Key parameters include pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrients. Farmers should apply balanced fertilizers based on SHC advice rather than using only urea, to improve yield and soil health.

Krishi Vigyan Kendras provide district-level support including soil testing, crop advisories, demonstration trials, and farmer training. Farmers should use KVK and state agriculture university advisories for local weather-based recommendations on seed variety, nutrient management, and pest control.

Minimum Support Price is announced by the Government of India for selected crops to protect farmers from distress sales. MSP procurement operations are season and state dependent. Farmers should check procurement centers, quality norms, and registration timelines with state agencies before bringing produce for sale.

Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana offers crop insurance against yield losses due to natural calamities, pests, and diseases. Farmer premium is typically 2 percent for Kharif crops, 1.5 percent for Rabi crops, and 5 percent for commercial or horticulture crops, with remaining premium subsidized by governments.

PM-KISAN provides income support of Rs 6000 per year to eligible farmer families in three equal instalments of Rs 2000 each. The amount is transferred directly to bank accounts through DBT. Farmers should complete eKYC, Aadhaar-bank seeding, and land record verification to avoid payment delays.
